query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a thin, continuous Al₂O₃ surface layer on boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by acting as an effective chemical barrier between the molten aluminum and the underlying boride matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components (e.g., high-entropy or conventional metal diborides) fabricated by methods such as spark plasma sintering, which typically exhibit some oxide inclusions and moderate porosity on their surfaces.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation heat treatment in an oxygen-rich atmosphere at an optimized temperature (e.g., around 1600–1700 °C) and duration that promotes in situ formation of a dense, adherent Al₂O₃ layer on the component surface.
generation.conditions: The treated components will be exposed to molten aluminum conditions (e.g., immersion at temperatures near or above 660 °C under static or low-flow conditions) where the protective oxide must remain adherent and intact during thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous, dense Al₂O₃ scale (with minimal porosity and cracking) formed in situ on the boride surface.
generation.mechanism: The preformed Al₂O₃ layer acts as a chemical and physical barrier that prevents direct contact between the aggressive molten aluminum and the boride substrate. This barrier inhibits aluminum dissolution into the substrate and minimizes interfacial reactions, thereby reducing corrosion rates and associated degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated boride surfaces, the pre-oxidized components will show significantly reduced weight change (indicating lower corrosion rates), less microstructural degradation, and improved surface integrity when exposed to molten aluminum over a fixed testing period.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with conventional surfaces (i.e., not subjected to the tailored pre-oxidation heat treatment) exposed under identical molten-aluminum conditions.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to hold provided that the oxidation treatment parameters yield an intact, adherent Al₂O₃ scale that does not spall under thermal or mechanical stresses; performance may deteriorate if the scale develops porosity, cracks, or poor adhesion during prolonged exposure or thermal cycling.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extrapolates from evidence of protective oxide layer formation in high-entropy borides (as in PMC10608203::web::018::5_conclusions) and from studies showing coated systems (PMC10488483::web::016::4_conclusions) that form dense refractory oxide scales. What is novel here is the intentional pre-oxidation to form an Al₂O₃ layer specifically for molten-aluminum corrosion protection—a condition not directly studied in either work—and the long-term adhesion and integrity of such a scale under molten aluminum is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based test coupons. Subject one set to the pre-oxidation heat treatment (e.g., 1600–1700 °C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for an optimized duration) to form the Al₂O₃ scale, while leaving the other set untreated. Then immerse both groups in molten aluminum under controlled laboratory conditions (e.g., at ~700 °C) for a fixed duration (e.g., 5 hours). After exposure, cool the samples and characterize the surfaces and cross-sections.
measurements: Weight change measurements to determine corrosion rate.
SEM/EDS analysis of cross-sectional microstructure to assess the integrity and thickness of the oxide scale and any evidence of molten-aluminum penetration.
XRD or other phase identification methods to confirm the presence and continuity of Al₂O₃ versus any reaction products at the interface.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (e.g., similar weight gain/loss, oxide spallation, or depth of substrate degradation) compared to the untreated samples under identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application. The paper presents the results of obtaining single-phase high-entropy ceramic materials with a high degree of chemical homogeneity using the equiatomic high-entropy boride (TiZrHfTaNb)B2 as an example. Single-phase and chemically homogeneous high-entropy borides were obtained by preliminary mixing of metals at the atomic level. The results of process research of mechanical alloying of TiZrHfTaNb showed that a homogeneous chemical composition with the lowest iron content (0.12%) was achieved with the following mechanical alloying modes: a rotation of the planetary disk/pots was 200–400 rpm and a process time was of 7.5 h. During sintering at temperatures around 1600 °C, a high-entropy boride with the chemical formula MeB2 is formed. Inclusions in the form of zirconium-hafnium oxide and a transition layer between oxide inclusions and the main boride phase are formed on the surface. Increasing the process temperature to 2000 °C leads to the formation of single-phase and chemically homogeneous high-entropy boride (TiZrHfTaNb)B2.
